newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Transcom sees 2nd half profit.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Transcom sees 2nd half profit.

text.p: Transcom International Ltd expects to be profitable in the second half of its fiscal year ending June 30, 1997, as production begins on diesel replacement engines using its natural gas vehicle system, Managing Director Peter Malone told Reuters.
That would leave the company about breakeven for all of fiscal 1997, he said in an interview, adding he expects Transcom "will be significantly profitable" in fiscal 1998.
The company had a fiscal 1996 loss of AUS$8.1 million after a writeoff of nearly $6 million, Malone said.

The writeoff brought Transco's Australian accounting into alignment with the practices of its international partners, he said, adding the change also cleared the way for Nasdaq trading of Transcom's shares, which began October 1.
He said the charges include the writeoff of about AUS$5.4 million of technology assets reflecting research that has not yet borne fruit and some $500,000 for the Nasdaq listing.

The loss came on revenues of $2.6 million, he said, explaining about half of these came from contract research and the rest from sales of the company's wireless data communications technology, Malone said.
Full details on fiscal 1996 will be available late this month when Transcom publishes its annual report.
He said production of heavy duty engines using Transcom's natural gas vehicle system is expected to begin March 1 at RABA Motor Co's Hungarian factory.

This "will start our cash flow" from the system, he pointed out. The technology allows production of a natural gas-fueled engine that mimics a diesel engine's performance curve while meeting ever-stricter emission requirements.
The resulting engines "have all the benefits of diesel and better," Malone said, noting they are much quieter than diesel engines and use a "fundamentally cheaper fuel."
Transcom is seeking license fees supported by royalties for the technology, which is expected to add US$1,000 to $2,000 to the cost of a heavy duty engine, he said.

Under its agreement with RABA, Transcom is receiving AUS$8,000 per engine for the first production batch of 600 units, Malone said, explaining the company is providing hardware as well as technology for these engines.
For the first 600 units, he said, Transcom is subcontracting the hardware. For future RABA sales, the company hopes to find a European manufacturer to supply the engine marker directly.

He said the company's AUS$3 million contract with the government of Western Australia to supply 100 natural gas fueled Renault SA heavy duty engines for city transit service is entering the third of four stages and will shortly begin actual production. Transcom also has alliances with
LucasVarity Plc's Perkins diesel unit for the use of technology.

Malone explained that both the natural gas vehicle system and Transcom's wireless data transmission technology are based on the company's process control patents, which describe both software and hardware. -- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610
